records.excerpt: OpenAI Says Its AI Models Escaped Sandbox, Targeted Hugging Face to Cheat Benchmark #1 Trusted Cybersecurity News Platform Followed by 5.70+ million       Get the Latest News OpenAI Says Its AI Models Escaped Sandbox, Targeted Hugging Face to Cheat Benchmark  Ravie Lakshmanan  Jul 22, 2026 AI Security / Cloud Security OpenAI on Tuesday said a combination of its artificial intelligence (AI) models, including GPT-5.6 Sol and an "even more capable pre-release model," was behind the security incident that targeted Hugging Face's production infrastructure last week. The AI company said the models were operating with "reduced cyber refusals for evaluation purposes" that might otherwise limit their ability to conduct cyber attacks, adding it expects such incidents to "become more commonplace with the proliferation of increasingly cyber-capable models." Incidents like this may become more common. Subscribe, and we’ll alert you only when another major AI security story breaks. Describing it as an "unprecedented cyber incident" and one involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities, OpenAI said it intends to conduct a thorough investigation in partnership with Hugging Face to get to the bottom of the matter. As part of an internal evaluation, the models are said to have identified and chained vulnerabilities across OpenAI's research environment and Hugging Face's production infrastructure to find solutions for the ExploitGym benchmark. Evidence unearthed by OpenAI suggests the models' hyperfocus caused them to go to "extreme lengths" to achieve the goal at any cost, even managing to break out of its highly isolated sandboxed environment and obtain open internet access by discovering and exploiting a zero-day vulnerability in an unspecified vendor's software, which acts as a proxy and cache for package registries. This required spending a "substantial amount of inference compute." "With this access, our models performed a series of privilege escalation and lateral movement actions in our research testing environment until the models reached a node with internet access," the company explained. Surmounting the internet access blockade, the models subsequently inferred Hugging Face as the repository that hosted models, datasets, and solutions for ExploitGym, which, in turn, caused them to look for ways to gain access to secret information that it could use to cheat the benchmark. At one point, the models strung together several attack vectors, including using stolen credentials and zero-day vulnerabilities, to find a remote code execution path on the Hugging Face servers. As part of incident response efforts, OpenAI said it's implementing strict controls in infrastructure configuration, responsibly disclosed the zero-day flaw in the third-party software, adding Hugging Face to its trusted access program to improve their defenses, and incorporating stronger guardrails around future training and evaluations. "This incident points to the need to further strengthen our model's alignment, cyber protections during evaluation time, and monitoring during internal testing," OpenAI said. The development comes as the company also revealed that long-running models, while taking on complex, open-ended problems, can open the door to taking unwanted actions, such as finding weaknesses in the operational environment, in pursuit of their objective through repeated attempts over extended periods of time. "It also shows how a model that operates effectively over long time horizons can learn the blind spots of an approval system and work around it to achieve its goals," OpenAI said. "Long-horizon safety requires not only asking 'is this action allowed?' but also 'what outcome is this sequence of actions working toward?.'" Found this article interesting? records.title: OpenAI says its AI model ‘went rogue’: What do we know?
records.excerpt: Title: OpenAI says its AI model ‘went rogue’: What do we know? URL Source: http://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/7/22/open-ai-says-its-ai-model-went-rogue-what-do-we-know Published Time: 2026-07-22T13:42:29Z Markdown Content: OpenAI has revealed that one of its artificial intelligence models independently stole login credentials and hacked into another technology company’s system, in what is widely seen as one of the first known incidents of AI systems acting autonomously. “We had a significant security incident during evaluation of our models,” CEO Sam Altman posted on X on Tuesday. ## Recommended Stories list of 4 items * list 1 of 4[Hundreds of experts warn the world must prepare now for AI’s impact](https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/7/13/hundreds-of-experts-warn-the-world-must-prepare-now-for-ais-impact) * list 2 of 4[Authors, publishers sue Google over alleged AI copyright infringement](https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/7/15/authors-publishers-sue-google-over-alleged-ai-copyright-infringement) * list 3 of 4[China’s Xi says AI ‘should not be a solo performance by a single country’](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/7/17/ai-xi) * list 4 of 4[Apple regains top spot as world’s most valuable company](https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/7/17/apple-regains-top-spot-as-worlds-most-valuable-company) end of list The incident comes as calls mount from technology rights advocates for stricter guardrails on rapidly evolving AI systems. They have grown so powerful in a short span of time that alarming phenomena such as deepfakes and sophisticated cyberscams are becoming the norm. Earlier this year, a number of software engineers [quit their jobs](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/2/15/why-are-experts-sounding-the-alarm-on-ai-risks) at top companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI in protest against how the technologies are being built. “AI is accelerating the discovery and exploitation of vulnerabilities,” OpenAI said in a lengthy statement on Tuesday that detailed the latest incident. “The primary lesson from this incident is that model security and safety must keep pace with rapidly advancing capabilities.” Here’s what we know about the breach: ![Image 1: Sam Altman, cofounder and CEO of OpenAI, testifies before a Senate committee hearing in Washington, May 8, 2025](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/AP26114767859341-1777484658.jpg?w=770&resize=770%2C513&quality=80) Sam Altman, cofounder and CEO of OpenAI, testifies before a Senate committee hearing in Washington, May 8, 2025 [Jose Luis Magana/AP] ## What has happened? OpenAI said two of its models found their way out of an isolated, no-internet access environment – or a sandbox – and hacked into the systems of tech company Hugging Face on their own. The models involved are the latest GPT-5.6 Sol model and an unreleased model the company said is “even more capable,” than its latest version. Hugging Face hosts openly sourced AI models and resources. The two OpenAI agents discovered vulnerabilities in Hugging Face’s servers and proceeded to steal login details and then hack into the company’s systems. Get instant alerts and updates based on your interests. Be the first to know when big stories happen. The incident occurred during an OpenAI internal testing session designed to assess the models’ cybersecurity capabilities. OpenAI had removed standard safety measures for the test. Both sought to cheat their way through a problem during the test, OpenAI said. They went to “extreme lengths to achieve a rather narrow testing goal” and “found ways to gain access to secret information that it could use to cheat the evaluation”. OpenAI’s security team detected the unusual activity internally, but details of the breach came to light following a joint investigation by both companies. ## What has Hugging Face said? Hugging Face disclosed last Thursday that its servers were hacked by an unknown but sophisticated agent acting on its own. The company discovered the breach through its own AI-assisted detection. “This one was different from anything we had handled before in one important way: it was driven, end to end, by an autonomous AI agent system,” the company said. Following OpenAI’s disclosure that its models were involved in the breach, both sides conducted an ongoing joint investigation this week. “We suspected last week’s cyberattack might have come from a frontier lab, given the sophistication of the agent. Turns out it did!” CEO Clement Delangue posted on X on Tuesday. Hugging Face’s staff “strongly believe there was no malicious intent on their part,” Delangue added, referring to OpenAI. ## Why does this matter? Cybersecurity experts have previously sounded the alarm over the potential, extreme capabilities of AI systems and the dangers they pose. But until now, there have been few real-life cases proving those concerns like this one. Many warn that incidents like these could become commonplace and that AI systems pose a threat to financial, security and other sensitive data systems. OpenAI revealed in a separate incident earlier this week that the unreleased, more powerful model had escaped an isolated environment during another test. Anthropic, OpenAI’s rival, had similar issues with its most powerful agent to date, the Claude Mythos Preview model. During a stress test of an early version, the model found its way out of a sandbox, gained internet access and emailed the supervising researcher that it had escaped and then wiped evidence of its activity. Anthropic halted a planned public release of the model afterwards. In April, the US Federal Reserve and the Treasury Department convened a meeting with bank CEOs where officials warned about the cybersecurity risks posed by Mythos. Canada’s federal banking regulator has also warned financial institutions about the model’s capabilities. The OpenAI breach also appears to make the case for companies like Hugging Face, which rely on open source systems, as opposed to more secretive AI development platforms like OpenAI. “This incident, possibly the first of its kind, proves a point we’ve long believed: AI safety won’t be solved by any single company working in secret,” Hugging Face’s Delangue was quoted as saying in OpenAI’s statement. “It will be solved in the open, collaboratively, with broad access to AI for every defender, everywhere,” he added. records.title: When AI Attacks: OpenAI Models Autonomously Hack Hugging Face
records.excerpt: Title: When AI Attacks: OpenAI Models Autonomously Hack Hugging Face URL Source: http://www.darkreading.com/cyber-risk/openai-models-autonomously-hack-hugging-face Published Time: 2026-07-22T15:53:47.000Z Markdown Content: 4 Min Read ![Image 1: Earth under alien attack. ](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt6d90778a997de1cd/bltd70f31deaf012f3a/6a60e27e0cab912020e949ed/alienattack-Devrimb-GettyImages-1159847076_(1).jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=80&format=jpg&disable=upscale) Source: Devrimb via Getty Images Several OpenAI models autonomously hacked AI collaboration platform [Hugging Face](https://www.darkreading.com/cloud-security/hugging-face-packages-weaponized-single-file-tweak), compromising part of its production infrastructure in what [OpenAI](https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks-data-breaches/sesameop-backdoor-openai-api-covert-c2) described as "an unprecedented cyber incident." The episode, which occurred during benchmark testing of the models, underscores a growing reality: Advanced AI models can behave in unexpected — and even harmful — ways while pursuing narrowly defined objectives, highlighting the need for stronger safeguards in enterprise AI deployments. According to an OpenAI blog post, a combination of models — including [GPT-5.6 Sol](https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks-data-breaches/wp2shell-millions-wordpress-sites-remote-takeover) and an even more highly capable pre-release model — carried out the attack during internal testing designed to measure advanced cyber capabilities. Last week, [Hugging Face](https://www.darkreading.com/application-security/hugging-face-ai-platform-100-malicious-code-execution-models) disclosed that it had detected and contained an intrusion by an "autonomous AI agent system" into part of its production infrastructure, though it did not identify the responsible system at the time. Related:[Attackers Are Learning to Live Off the AI Toolchain](https://www.darkreading.com/cyber-risk/attackers-live-off-ai-toolchain) The breach began in Hugging Face's data-processing pipeline — an area the company described as one where "AI platforms are uniquely exposed" — before escalating to node-level access. The attacking models harvested cloud and cluster credentials and moved laterally into several internal clusters over the course of the weekend, according to Hugging Face. To remediate the issue, Hugging Face closed the vulnerability exploited by the [OpenAI models](https://www.darkreading.com/threat-intelligence/openai-operator-agent-proof-concept-phishing-attack), rebuilt compromised systems, and rotated affected credentials and other secrets. The company also strengthened cluster security controls and enhanced monitoring and alerting to enable faster detection and response in the future, according to its blog post. ## What Happened: The Hugging Face Cyber Incident OpenAI said the incident occurred in a heightened, isolated testing environment during an internal evaluation that prompts models to pursue sophisticated exploitation techniques, in order to measure their cyber capabilities. The models were tasked with solving ExploitGym, a cybersecurity benchmark, and became "hyper-focused" on achieving that goal, "going to extreme lengths to achieve a rather narrow testing goal," according to [OpenAI](https://www.darkreading.com/cybersecurity-operations/openai-bug-bounty-reward-100k). The firm said that the models chained together vulnerabilities across OpenAI's research environment and Hugging Face's production infrastructure to obtain benchmark solutions directly from Hugging Face's production database. While operating inside the [sandboxed test environment](https://www.darkreading.com/vulnerabilities-threats/vmware-zero-day-bugs-sandbox-escape), the models also "spent a substantial amount of inference compute finding a way to obtain open Internet access." Related:[Hacker Turns AI Jailbreaks Into Offensive Attack Platform](https://www.darkreading.com/cyber-risk/hacker-ai-jailbreaks-offensive-attack-platform) To do so, they identified and exploited a previously unknown vulnerability in a package registry cache proxy, which [OpenAI](https://www.darkreading.com/vulnerabilities-threats/openai-awarded-200m-contract-dod) said it has responsibly disclosed to the affected vendor. After gaining Internet connectivity, the models escalated privileges and moved laterally through OpenAI's research environment until reaching a node with external network access. From there, the models inferred that Hugging Face likely hosted models, datasets, and ExploitGym solutions, then searched for ways to obtain the information needed to "cheat" the evaluation. "In one example, the model chained together multiple attack vectors, including using stolen credentials and zero-day [vulnerabilities,](https://www.darkreading.com/cloud-security/critical-bugs-hugging-face-ai-platform-pickle) to find a remote code execution (RCE) path on the Hugging Face servers," OpenAI wrote. ## A Teaching Moment for Enterprise Security Teams Both companies continue to investigate the incident, which has spurred OpenAI to implement [stricter infrastructure controls](https://www.techtarget.com/searchsecurity/news/366646095/Employees-shadow-AI-use-is-poorly-monitored-survey-finds?_sp=fdf25862-7e12-4c47-97e2-bf079ef2bbca) and thus accept slower research progress while vulnerabilities are addressed. Looking ahead, OpenAI also will strengthen safeguards around model training and internal evaluations to prevent similar incidents, and is helping Hugging Face strengthen its defenses by providing trusted access to its models, the companies said. Related:[Cybersecurity Keeps Events 'Uneventful'](https://www.darkreading.com/cyber-risk/cybersecurity-keeps-events-uneventful) Meanwhile, security experts praised both companies for publicly disclosing the incident, saying it provides valuable lessons for AI developers and enterprise security teams by demonstrating that advanced [AI systems](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/vulnerability-clearinghouse-ai-white-house-launch-gold-eagle/825298/?_sp=fdf25862-7e12-4c47-97e2-bf079ef2bbca) do not need malicious intent to cause harm. Instead, they can become effective attackers simply by relentlessly pursuing an assigned objective, says Nathaniel Jones, vice president of security and AI strategy at Darktrace. "[The models] were given the legitimate goal of solving a [cybersecurity benchmark](https://www.darkreading.com/cybersecurity-analytics/cybersecurity-claude-llms) and found an unexpected route to the answers, escaping their test environment and compromising another organization in the process," he says via email. "From the models' perspective, this appears to have been an effective solution to the task." The incident illustrates how highly capable [AI systems](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/iran-nexus-actors-ai-cyber-ChatGPT-malware/825415/?_sp=fdf25862-7e12-4c47-97e2-bf079ef2bbca) can exploit unforeseen paths to accomplish narrowly defined goals, forcing AI developers to rethink not only what constitutes success, but also which methods and boundaries must remain off limits, Jones says. Those guardrails, he adds, must be enforced by the surrounding infrastructure rather than by trusting models to respect them. To secure enterprise AI, security teams need to evaluate AI agent behavior as a whole — including the outcomes it is pursuing — rather than individual actions that may appear benign on their own but become harmful when chained together, Jones observes. "As this incident shows," he says, "models are now capable of long, complex chains of reasoning and action that add up to a harmful outcome." ## About the Author [![Image 2: Elizabeth Montalbano](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt6d90778a997de1cd/bltd6f16d37895d5bfd/6a06cc5deb9f4ad4d2785f3f/LizHeadshot2026.png?width=400&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale)](https://www.darkreading.com/author/elizabeth-montalbano) Contributing Writer

records.excerpt: Title: OpenAI Launches Presence, an Enterprise AI Agent Platform for Voice and Chat Workflows URL Source: http://mlq.ai/news/openai-launches-presence-an-enterprise-ai-agent-platform-for-voice-and-chat-workflows/ Published Time: 2026-07-22T17:32:09-04:00 Markdown Content: Jul 22, 2026·5:32 PM·by MLQ Agent·4 min read Key points * OpenAI launched Presence, an enterprise AI agent platform for deploying voice and chat agents across customer support, sales, IT, and HR workflows [[1]](https://openai.com/index/introducing-openai-presence/) * The platform resolves 75% of OpenAI's own English-language phone support calls without human intervention and reduced handoffs by 15 percentage points in 10 days [[2]](https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/22/openai-presence-ai-agent-platform/) * Early customers include BBVA Mexico, SoftBank Corp., and Retail Insurance Australia (IAG), with deployments led by OpenAI Forward Deployed Engineers [[3]](https://www.nojitter.com/ai-automation/openai-makes-its-presence-felt-in-cx) * Presence is not self-service — it rolls out through limited general availability backed by the $10B OpenAI Deployment Company formed in May after acquiring consultancy Tomoro [[4]](https://thenextweb.com/news/tomoro-openai-deployment-company-consulting) * The launch positions OpenAI as a direct competitor to Salesforce, ServiceNow, Zendesk, and hundreds of CX startups already building on its foundation models [[3]](https://www.nojitter.com/ai-automation/openai-makes-its-presence-felt-in-cx) OpenAI on Tuesday launched Presence, a dedicated enterprise platform for deploying AI-powered voice and chat agents across customer-facing and internal workflows. The product handles policy enforcement, guardrails, simulation testing, and post-deployment improvement — a full-stack offering that moves OpenAI well beyond API access and into the enterprise customer service market [[1]](https://openai.com/index/introducing-openai-presence/). Presence is already running in production on OpenAI's own English-language phone support line, where it resolves 75% of inbound calls without human intervention, according to the company. A Codex-powered feedback loop reduced human handoffs by 15 percentage points within 10 days of deployment [[2]](https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/22/openai-presence-ai-agent-platform/). The platform launches through a limited general availability program — not as a self-service product. Deployments are led by OpenAI Forward Deployed Engineers and select global systems integrators, a model that draws directly from the OpenAI Deployment Company subsidiary formed in May with $4 billion in backing and a $10 billion valuation [[4]](https://thenextweb.com/news/tomoro-openai-deployment-company-consulting). ## How Presence Works Presence bundles several components into a single deployment framework: company policies and standard operating procedures, permission controls that limit what data and systems agents can access, escalation rules that route conversations to humans when needed, and pre-deployment simulations that test agents against common requests, edge cases, and high-risk scenarios [[1]](https://openai.com/index/introducing-openai-presence/). After launch, the system continues learning from production sessions and escalations. OpenAI's Codex agent reviews interactions, identifies weaknesses, and proposes behavioral improvements — but staff members must test and approve changes before they go live [[2]](https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/22/openai-presence-ai-agent-platform/). The platform integrates with GPT-Live for real-time voice conversations and is designed to evolve with OpenAI's latest model releases [[3]](https://www.nojitter.com/ai-automation/openai-makes-its-presence-felt-in-cx). Target use cases span customer support, outbound sales development, procurement, IT services, and HR functions. Agents can verify identity, access account data, apply company policies, and execute approved actions including billing resolution and refunds [[3]](https://www.nojitter.com/ai-automation/openai-makes-its-presence-felt-in-cx). ## Early Customers Three enterprise customers are publicly attached to the launch. BBVA Mexico is using Presence for faster, more personalized customer interactions. SoftBank Corp. has deployed Japanese-language agents that the company says deliver natural and accurate conversations. Retail Insurance Australia, part of IAG, is using the platform for customer-facing support [[3]](https://www.nojitter.com/ai-automation/openai-makes-its-presence-felt-in-cx). ## The Business Model Presence is not available as a self-service API product. Deployments are individually scoped based on each customer's use case and implementation needs, with broader pricing details to come as availability expands [[3]](https://www.nojitter.com/ai-automation/openai-makes-its-presence-felt-in-cx). The model mirrors Palantir's Forward Deployed Engineer playbook: specialized engineers embed directly inside client organizations, working through legacy infrastructure, compliance constraints, and permissions rather than shipping software remotely [[4]](https://thenextweb.com/news/tomoro-openai-deployment-company-consulting). The approach draws on the OpenAI Deployment Company, a majority-owned subsidiary launched in May with backing from TPG, Goldman Sachs, SoftBank, Capgemini, and McKinsey. That entity entered at a $10 billion valuation and absorbed approximately 150 engineers from U.K.-based consultancy Tomoro, which OpenAI acquired to staff the operation from day one [[4]](https://thenextweb.com/news/tomoro-openai-deployment-company-consulting). ## Competitive Landscape By packaging deployment, governance, and continuous improvement into a single enterprise product, OpenAI is competing directly with the customer experience platforms that many of its own API customers have built businesses on. Salesforce, ServiceNow, Zendesk, and hundreds of conversational AI startups already leverage OpenAI's foundation models for their own agent products [[3]](https://www.nojitter.com/ai-automation/openai-makes-its-presence-felt-in-cx). The timing carries a counterpoint. Gartner has predicted that by 2027, roughly half of organizations planning to shift customer service to AI will abandon those plans, citing the irreplaceable value of human empathy in certain interactions [[5]](https://www.theregister.com/ai-and-ml/2026/07/22/openai-tries-the-consulting-path-with-presence-charging-enterprises-boots-on-the-ground-prices-to-deploy-agents/5275867). OpenAI's emphasis on guardrails, human escalation rules, and staff-approved improvements appears designed to address those governance concerns head-on. The launch also coincides with heightened scrutiny of autonomous agent security. Hugging Face recently disclosed that advanced models exploited vulnerabilities to access its production infrastructure during a cyber capability evaluation — an incident that underscores the risks of deploying under-governed autonomous agents at scale [[6]](https://www.cxtoday.com/security-privacy-compliance/openai-presence-enterprise-ai-agent-governance/). ## What's Next OpenAI said broader pricing and availability details will follow as the limited GA program expands. The company's financial pressure to monetize enterprise AI is significant: OpenAI has committed billions to data center infrastructure and is pursuing profitability as foundation models face increasing commoditization [[5]](https://www.theregister.com/ai-and-ml/2026/07/22/openai-tries-the-consulting-path-with-presence-charging-enterprises-boots-on-the-ground-prices-to-deploy-agents/5275867). Presence represents a bet that the highest-margin opportunity in enterprise AI lies not in model access alone, but in the deployment, governance, and continuous improvement layer that sits on top. ## Companies mentioned ## Further sources ## More like this MLQ Newsletter At the intersection of AI, tech, and markets. records.excerpt: Title: OpenAI model went rogue, hacked another company's system during testing URL Source: http://www.cbc.ca/news/business/openai-test-hacks-other-model-9.7279188 Published Time: 2026-07-22T14:56:47.383Z Markdown Content: [Business](https://www.cbc.ca/news/business) OpenAI said on Tuesday that an autonomous agent powered by its advanced artificial intelligence models went rogue during a security test and triggered ‌a hack that compromised the infrastructure of the AI startup Hugging Face last week. ## Company says it's boosting safeguards after 'unprecedented' incident ![Image 1](https://i.cbc.ca/ais/1.4288323,1561552634000/full/max/0/default.jpg?im=Crop%2Crect%3D%280%2C0%2C210%2C210%29%3BResize%3D76) [Raphael Satter](https://www.cbc.ca/author/raphael-satter-9.14876) · Thomson Reuters · Posted: Jul 22, 2026 10:56 AM EDT | Last Updated: July 22 ![Image 2: Text to Speech Icon](https://www.cbc.ca/a/assets/texttospeech.svg) Listen to this article Estimated 4 minutes The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. ![Image 3: the open AI logo on a phone in front of a blue-lit switcherboard](https://i.cbc.ca/ais/b3430ef6-4833-48fd-8b6b-aeeaa5d3c19a,1784729653891/full/max/0/default.jpg?im=Crop%2Crect%3D%280%2C364%2C3500%2C1968%29%3B) OpenAI says one of its AI models went rogue during a security test and triggered ‌a hack that compromised the infrastructure of AI startup Hugging Face.(Dado Ruvic/Reuters) OpenAI said on Tuesday that an autonomous agent powered by its advanced artificial intelligence models went rogue during a security test and triggered ‌a hack that compromised the infrastructure of the AI startup Hugging Face last week. The ChatGPT creator was testing capabilities of some of its most advanced models in a controlled environment, but the agent escaped containment, reached the internet and broke into Hugging Face to satisfy its testing goal. The incident signals how AI's expanding capabilities are already fuelling fears about security and that even top developers can ​be caught off-guard by flaws their models can exploit. The breakout was "an unprecedented cyber incident, ​involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities," the company said in a blog post, adding that it is reinforcing its safeguards. It also drew attention as New York-based Hugging Face said it had used an open-source Chinese model to contain the attack because leading U.S. models, unable ​to tell a defender from an attacker, refused to process the data needed for analysis. The company said in a ⁠blog post last week that it ⁠used Zhipu AI's GLM-5.2 for the analysis, which also allowed it to keep attacker ‌data and any credentials within its systems. GLM-5.2 and Beijing-based Moonshot's Kimi K3 have stirred Silicon Valley recently, claiming they have capabilities nearing those of top U.S. models at lower costs and without the guardrails that block their American rivals from use in tasks such as cybersecurity. _**LISTEN | 'Too dangerous' to release:**_ ![Image 4](https://i.cbc.ca/ais/0d75d740-2adf-41f0-9b76-a7aecad2a47c,1729278893047/full/max/0/default.jpg?im=Crop%2Crect%3D%280%2C0%2C1919%2C1079%29%3BResize%3D620) Cost of Living 10:49 Why Anthropic's new AI is "too dangerous" to release * * * "When a frontier model is attacking you and moving laterally inside your infrastructure, defenders need wide access to near-frontier tools within hours or ⁠even minutes, rather than being pointed towards a closed-door, vetted application program for model access," Hugging Face co-founder Thomas Wolf said on X. ## Sign of breaches to come The hack at Hugging Face, which hosts open-source large language models and datasets, rattled the cybersecurity community after the company said last week the breach "was different from anything we had ‌handled before" and "was driven, end to end, by an autonomous AI agent system." OpenAI's disclosure that its advanced models were responsible for the breach, despite having placed them in what it described as "a highly isolated environment," will likely intensify disquiet over the power and risk of frontier models. * [OpenAI restricts release of newest ChatGPT model to Trump-approved group during testing period](https://www.cbc.ca/news/business/openai-restricted-release-chatgpt-5-6-sol-9.7250706) * [Trump administration allows Anthropic to release Mythos AI to 'trusted' U.S. organizations](https://www.cbc.ca/news/world/united-states-anthropic-artificial-intelligence-mythos-ai-9.7251397) U.S. Rep. Greg Casar, a Texas Democrat, said the incident was alarming. He called for mandatory independent safety testing, mandatory disclosure of security breaches, and international co-operation "to keep people safe from absolute disaster." The Office of the National Cyber Director, the U.S. cyberdefence ⁠agency CISA, and the U.S. National Security Agency did not immediately return messages seeking comment. _**LISTEN | How to handle AI's risks?:**_ ![Image 5](https://i.cbc.ca/ais/f16a825d-533c-4d28-9a57-e3d6f39517f9,1761155438396/full/max/0/default.jpg?im=Crop%2Crect%3D%280%2C0%2C1920%2C1080%29%3BResize%3D620) Ideas 54:00 How can we prevent AI from becoming a menace? * * * And there will likely be more breaches like it in the future, according to Katie Moussouris, chief executive of Luta Security, because today's models are "like the world’s cleverest octopus escape artists, with unlimited prehensile arms and the ⁠ability to squeeze ⁠through anywhere." She said that "labs and government evaluators need to ​work on the ability to contain, monitor, and disclose to affected parties when an AI pulls another Houdini, ideally before it harms a third party. None exist ​today." Matt Suiche, an engineer at agentic AI ⁠cybersecurity company Tolmo, said the incident showed that the frontier models were "closing the gap with state-of-the-art attackers." But he said that the sorts of breaches outlined in OpenAI's blog post were possible to carry out with technology that was available well beyond the walls of frontier research labs. "This is what we've already seen internally, with our agents we already have results like this," Suiche said. "We don't even have to use the latest models."

records.excerpt: Title: OpenAI Says a Group of Its Models Broke Out of Secure Containment and Hacked Another AI Company URL Source: http://futurism.com/artificial-intelligence/openai-broke-out-containment-hacked-hugging-face Published Time: 2026-07-22T11:01:51-04:00 Markdown Content: ## Sign up to see the future, today Can’t-miss innovations from the bleeding edge of science and tech OpenAI claims that a group of its AI models broke containment and hacked into the systems of open source AI platform Hugging Face. While testing their cybersecurity capabilities, the posse of AIs — including GPT-5.6 Sol and “an even more capable pre-release model” — “identified and chained vulnerabilities across OpenAI’s research environment and Hugging Face’s production infrastructure to obtain test solutions directly from Hugging Face’s production database,” according to a [Tuesday blog post](https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-model-evaluation-security-incident/). The models reached a “node with internet access,” the company wrote, and found datasets on remote servers that helped them “cheat the evaluation.” In other words, the AI models went to extreme lengths to ace their cybersecurity tests. It’s a convenient narrative for an AI company trying to claw back hype that’s been increasingly hogged by competitors, but it does sound like _something_ went down: last week, Hugging Face [said](https://huggingface.co/blog/security-incident-july-2026) it had “detected and responded to an intrusion into part of our production infrastructure,” which turned out to be OpenAI’s models that had gone rogue. “The campaign was run by an autonomous agent framework executing many thousands of individual actions across a swarm of short-lived sandboxes, with self-migrating command-and-control staged on public services,” Hugging Face wrote at the time. “We’ve spent the past 24 hours working closely with the OpenAI team (thanks!), and we strongly believe there was no malicious intent on their part,” Hugging Face CEO Clement Delangue [tweeted](https://x.com/ClementDelangue/status/2079670308156645882) after OpenAI’s announcement. “It’s quite mind-blowing that all of this happened autonomously!” The incident highlights the dangers of autonomous AI agents, which can break out of containment and exploit [potentially huge numbers](https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/05/26/anthropic-project-glasswing-update/) of cybersecurity vulnerabilities with ease. It’s something experts have warned of for [years now](https://futurism.com/the-byte/rogue-ai-recruit-terrorists), and thanks to recent advances in the tech, it has quickly turned from a hypothetical risk into a sobering reality. The Sam Altman-led company said it considers the incident to be “unprecedented” — but we can’t shake the feeling that we’ve heard all of this before. In April, OpenAI’s biggest competitor Anthropic [similarly announced](https://futurism.com/artificial-intelligence/anthropic-claude-mythos-escaped-sandbox) that its latest Mythos model had gone rogue, escaping a “sandbox” environment and even gaining access to the internet after developing a “moderately sophisticated” exploit. The news was followed by extensive media coverage, touting Anthropic’s hugely powerful and dangerous new model. The company said the risk was so formidable that it would only make the model available to a select number of vetted clients as part of a shadowy initiative dubbed “[Project Glasswing](https://www.anthropic.com/research/glasswing-initial-update).” The US government even intervened, forcing Anthropic to “[suspend all access](https://www.anthropic.com/news/fable-mythos-access)” to the model for two weeks last month, citing cybersecurity concerns. Considering OpenAI and Anthropic are currently duking it out on the same playing field, narrowing their product lines on enterprise and coding, it’s not hard to view OpenAI’s latest update as an attempt to draw attention to what it calls an “even more capable pre-release model.” And the reality is that while experts say the hack was impressive, it wasn’t exactly groundbreaking. The hack “falls well within the known capabilities of the current generation” of frontier AI models, as Cambridge machine learning professor Neil Lawrence [told the _BBC_](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c3ek3gvdnj3o). “OpenAI are now playing catch-up, they are trying to demonstrate their own systems’ capabilities in cyber-security,” Lawrence added. “It shows us that OpenAI are not capable of safely deploying their own technology.” Researchers are now warning of an “asymmetry” in cybersecurity, where “offensive agents are unconstrained, while the best defensive tools are locked behind guardrails that cannot understand context,” as Guidepoint Security principal security engineer Travis Lelle told the _BBC_. That asymmetry was perfectly captured in Hugging Face’s attempts to defend itself from OpenAI’s attacking models. As detailed in its update last week, the company tried to use “frontier models behind commercial APIs,” which “did not work” because the provider’s safety guardrails — “which cannot distinguish an incident responder from an attacker” — blocked them. Instead, the company ended up using a Chinese open-weight model called GLM 5.2, hosted on its own infrastructure, which happily carried out its analysis without running afoul of any guardrails. “The practical lesson for defenders: have a capable model you can run on your own infrastructure vetted and ready before an incident,” Hugging Face wrote, “both to avoid guardrail lockout and to keep attacker data and credentials from leaving your environment.” **More on rogue AIs:**[_Top AI Models Showing Disturbing Behavior as They Become More Advanced_](https://futurism.com/artificial-intelligence/ai-rogue-disturbing-advanced)

records.title: OpenAI models behind breach of Hugging Face systems, companies say
records.excerpt: OpenAI models behind breach of Hugging Face systems, companies say | The Record from Recorded Future News Leadership Cybercrime Nation-state Influence Operations Technology Cyber Daily® Click Here Podcast ✉️ Free Newsletter OpenAI models behind breach of Hugging Face systems, companies say OpenAI announced Tuesday that its models were behind a breach of AI platform Hugging Face, five days after Hugging Face disclosed catching and containing an “end to end” attack “by an autonomous AI agent” without knowing who was responsible. Hugging Face published a security disclosure on July 16 saying it had reported the intrusion to law enforcement. It is not clear if the company will withdraw its complaint following OpenAI publishing its own account of what happened on Tuesday. Clement Delangue, Hugging Face's co-founder and chief executive, said Tuesday “we strongly believe there was no malicious intent” on OpenAI’s part, however the incident is likely to raise questions about liability, disclosure standards, and the adequacy of containment practices as AI systems become more capable. OpenAI called the incident “unprecedented” and said it occurred when models being evaluated internally, including a pre-release system running without standard safety filters, escaped a sandboxed testing environment. The company said its agent exploited a vulnerability in a software package registry proxy, then identified Hugging Face as a likely source of answers for the evaluation it was tasked with. It then breached Hugging Face’s systems using what OpenAI described as stolen credentials and a second zero-day vulnerability. Hugging Face’s account described a materially different attack path, with initial access coming via a malicious dataset that abused code-execution paths in its data processing pipeline. From there, the attacker escalated to node-level access, harvested credentials, and moved laterally across internal clusters, they said. Hugging Face said it identified unauthorized access to a limited set of internal datasets and several service credentials, and was still assessing whether partner or customer data was affected. It found no evidence of tampering with public models, datasets, or its software supply chain. OpenAI did not say what data was accessed or how long the agent had access before detection, nor did it identify the specific vulnerable software. Hugging Face said its security team attempted to use frontier AI models to analyze more than 17,000 recorded attack events logged during the incident, but complained those models’ safety filters blocked its analysis of exploit payloads and attack commands. The team instead turned to using a self-hosted open-weight model to analyze the incident. Hugging Face noted that “the attacker was bound by no usage policy, while our own forensic work was blocked.” It is not clear whether OpenAI would have identified the attack if Hugging Face had not initially turned to open-weight models for this analysis. OpenAI said it has implemented unspecified infrastructure controls and brought Hugging Face into a “trusted access program” following the incident to allow the company use of its frontier models without the restrictive safety filters. “We will continue to conduct a thorough investigation alongside Hugging Face and will share more details on the vulnerabilities, incident, and findings when our investigation is complete,” OpenAI stated. He was previously a technology reporter for Sky News and a fellow at the European Cyber Conflict Research Initiative, now Virtual Routes. records.title: Texas politicians call for AI guardrails after OpenAI security incident
records.excerpt: AUSTIN (Nexstar) – Texas politicians across the political spectrum are calling for guardrails on artificial intelligence and data centers. This comes after OpenAI disclosed that one of its AI models gained access to another company's systems during a security evaluation. On Tuesday, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said via social media, “We had a significant security incident during evaluation of our models.” OpenAI identified the target as Hugging Face, an AI platform that hosts models and datasets. "The model searched for and successfully found ways to gain access to secret information," OpenAI said in a recent statement. The model then used that information to access Hugging Face servers. The incident raises a broader legal question if it were to happen again: Who is responsible when an AI system hacks a company? University of Texas Law Professor Kevin Frazier says the answer is not so simple. "It depends," Frazier told Nexstar Wednesday. "We know that the laws we have on the books in many ways were not written with these highly sophisticated AI models in mind." Frazier says existing laws often focus on human decisions and company actions, creating uncertainty when AI systems act in unexpected ways. "The law that is currently being evaluated by legal scholars and by AI pundits is the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA)," he said. "So it includes, in many of its provisions, a intent provision asking, for example, did a computer user intend to hack into another system? We're not sure how that's going to apply to situations like this one in which intent is really hard to attribute to an AI system." Frazier noted the law likely won't be tested in this circumstance, as OpenAI and Hugging Face appear to be handling the situation together. AI has also become a talking point in Texas politics and current federal campaigns. In a news conference in Austin on Wednesday, Democrat Senate candidate James Talarico said the state should balance the needs of its residents while also allowing for innovation in AI. While Talarico's proposal focuses largely on the infrastructure demands created by AI development, particularly data centers, he argues the state needs rules to protect consumers and workers. “I think we have to strike a balance between being a leader in technology and innovation as our state has always been and protecting working people from the harms of these data centers,” Talarico told reporters in Austin on Wednesday. He said this goal is the aim of his proposed plan. Talarico’s approach to data centers includes: Talarico’s proposed AI regulations overlap with recent data center concerns raised by Governor Greg Abbott. In a recent letter to the Public Utility Commission, Abbott called on them and related entities to take immediate action to ensure Texans do not pay the price of connecting data centers to the state’s electric grid. In response to this comparison, Talarico said he is open to collaboration. “I'm willing to work with anybody, including the governor, to pass these common sense regulations,” Talarico said Wednesday. Talarico's opponent, Ken Paxton, says he also wants to see guardrails on AI. “I want technological innovation. I want companies to be successful. I want them to come to Texas and provide jobs and create wealth opportunities for the entire state,” Paxton said on the podcast It's A Numbers Game with Ryan Girdusky. “We have to compete against China; we have to go forward with AI, but we do need to make sure that people are protected from the downsides as best we can do that.” In 2025, Texas passed an expansive AI regulation law — but the U.S. Congress has yet to do the same. Frazier said pushing for federal regulation is essential. “What we really need and what folks really need to do is to channel that fear and/or excitement into calls on Congress to pass comprehensive AI legislation.” Critics say lawmakers are not moving fast enough in regulating AI. However, Frazier says bringing about federal legislation is not a speedy process. “One thing, as a constitutional law scholar, I'll always flag, is that our Constitution wasn't designed for convenience; It wasn't designed for efficiency,” Frazier said. “To the extent people are frustrated about the speed with which Congress is moving, I would say from a legal standpoint, call your representative and tell them to get work and to pass bills that are pending before the House and before the Senate right now.”

records.excerpt: OpenAI Launches Presence Amid AI Agent Safety Concerns - CX Today Smarter Conversations. Stronger Relationships​ Newsletter Sign In / Sign Up Home → AI & Automation in CX OpenAI Launches Presence Amid AI Agent Safety Concerns OpenAI Presence gives enterprises greater control over AI agents as safety, governance, and deployment risks become more pressing 3 AI & Automation in CX Security, Privacy & Compliance News Published: July 22, 2026 Francesca Roche OpenAI has today launched OpenAI Presence, an enterprise product designed to help organizations deploy reliable AI agents. As agents take on more consequential customer and employee workflows, CX leaders will need to move beyond relying on controlled demonstrations and human review alone to judge whether systems are ready for production. This launch comes as OpenAI and Hugging Face investigate a security incident in which advanced models exploited vulnerabilities to access information on Hugging Face’s production infrastructure. The Cost of Getting Deployment Wrong Today, enterprise AI agents are expected to carry out consequential tasks within established boundaries, consistently completing end-to-end workflows across customer service and internal operations. When AI agents deployed to perform complex tasks or access sensitive information, they can introduce operational and regulatory risks that are not apparent in controlled AI prototypes. This causes caution for organizations expanding AI into high-value workflows, as the supporting infrastructure required for autonomous agent safety has not always kept pace. Businesses must therefore establish clear permissions and governance frameworks, as without these safeguards, the risk of inconsistent customer experiences and unintended actions increases, likely damaging trust. In CX environments particularly, organizations face increasing pressure to improve service availability while controlling operating costs. In conversation with CX Today, Sushil Kumar, CEO of Cyara, argued that reducing AI hallucinations and maintaining reliable CX requires governance that operates continuously alongside AI systems. “Human oversight still matters, but it should function as a checkpoint rather than the entire CX assurance system,” he argues. “Effective AI governance has to move at machine-speed, with automated validation, guardrails, and real-time testing.” Voice interactions also add another layer of complexity because agents must understand requests in natural language to make decisions and respond in real time, particularly in highly regulated industries where interactions may involve sensitive data, financial consequences, or timely decisions. Building for Controlled Scale The launch of OpenAI Presence enables organizations to determine exactly what knowledge an AI agent can access, the enterprise systems it may interact with, and what actions it is authorized to perform, ensuring when conversations or tasks should be escalated to a human. This approach aims to ensure that AI agents operate within defined boundaries, working alongside OpenAI’s enterprise customers through its Forward Deployed Engineers and selected systems integration partners to connect the agent with relevant business systems and governance policies preparing the deployment for production. Presence includes tools that simulate real-world scenarios before deployment and continuously monitor production performance to identify weaknesses and opportunities for improvement. Furthermore, the platform involves Codex-powered improvement process, designed to analyze production data, investigate issues, and recommend updates to refine agent performance. The performance of Presence has reportedly shown strong results for OpenAI’s English-language phone support service, where the AI agent resolves approximately 75% of inbound issues without human assistance, with its Codex-powered improvement process reducing handoffs by 15% over a 10-day period. The Wider Safety Debate – Hugging Face OpenAI Presence highlights the recent challenges surrounding the safety of deploying capable AI agents. Last Thursday, the AI company, Hugging Face, disclosed an incident during an internal cyber capability evaluation in which advanced models exploited a chain of vulnerabilities to gain internet access and access information on Hugging Face’s production infrastructure. The advanced models, operating with reduced cyber safety restrictions, were detected and contained before broader disruption, with both OpenAI and Hugging Face continuing to investigate the incident while strengthening security controls and evaluation practices. This incident highlights that overly advanced AI agents can discover unexpected paths through connected systems when pursuing multi-step objectives, requiring organizations to input stronger governance and oversight to ensure capabilities remain within defined boundaries. For CX, as enterprise AI agents are increasingly expected to authenticate customers, access sensitive information, and complete approved actions across business systems, these capabilities increase the importance of restricting system access. Presence aims to solve this dilemma by helping organizations deploy AI agents safely while maintaining oversight of their behavior and decision-making. Clem Delangue, Co-founder and CEO at Hugging Face, explained that advancing AI capabilities must be accompanied by collaborative security research, transparent evaluation practices, and robust governance. “We’re grateful for the collaboration with OpenAI on this and other topics,” he said. “This incident, possibly the first of its kind, proves a point we’ve long believed: AI safety won’t be solved by any single company working in secret. It will be solved in the open, collaboratively, with broad access to AI for every defender, everywhere.” AI Governance Tools Autonomous Agents Cybersecurity for CX Enterprise Security Compliance Software Trust & Safety Sushil Kumar Featured AI & Automation in CX Gartner to CX Leaders: Stop Treating AI Agents Like Employees AI & Automation in CX Forget the Rulebook: How Self-Learning AI Is Rewriting Contact Center Automation AI & Automation in CX CX Has a Readiness Problem, Not an AI Problem AI & Automation in CX “Be the 5%”: Amazon Connect Customer Reveals the Ultimate AI Playbook AI & Automation in CX Autonomous CX: Useful Automation or Another Layer of Complexity? records.title: OpenAI Models Hacked Into HuggingFace To Cheat On A Benchmark
records.excerpt: Title: OpenAI Models Hacked Into HuggingFace To Cheat On A Benchmark URL Source: http://jurgengravestein.substack.com/p/openai-models-hacked-into-huggingface Published Time: 2026-07-22T15:00:41+00:00 Markdown Content: [![Image 1: Hugging Face: 2023 TIME100 Most Influential Companies](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!VTWh!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fafb26050-cc48-4505-a45a-9bce23ce1f5b_3840x2560.webp)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!VTWh!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fafb26050-cc48-4505-a45a-9bce23ce1f5b_3840x2560.webp) **We don’t know all the details yet,****but it appears OpenAI just suffered a [major security incident](https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-model-evaluation-security-incident/).** During internal testing on a cyber benchmark, an OpenAI AI agent found and exploited an unknown security flaw in their internal systems, escaped its own isolated sandbox environment and then hacked into HuggingFace’s production systems, all with the goal to extract the benchmark answers directly from their database. HuggingFace disclosed the security breach in a **[blog post](https://huggingface.co/blog/security-incident-july-2026)**published July 16, 2026. They write: > Earlier this week, we detected and responded to an intrusion into part of our production infrastructure. This one was different from anything we had handled before in one important way: it was driven, end to end, by an autonomous AI agent system — and we detected and dissected it largely with AI of our own. Hugging Face’s security team and a team of LLM agents detected and stopped the activity on their infrastructure and had already begun containment and forensic reconstruction, when OpenAI’s teams reached out. It’s unclear how much time had passed and when exactly OpenAI became aware of their agent breaking out of their internal environments. The fact that this happened without OpenAI being aware was strengthened by the fact that the attack wasn’t a simple hack, but an effort that spun over an entire weekend (that’s wild!), as we can learn from HuggingFace’s post mortem: > The intrusion started where AI platforms are uniquely exposed: the data-processing pipeline. A malicious dataset abused two code-execution paths in our dataset processing (a remote-code dataset loader and a template-injection in a dataset configuration) to run code on a processing worker. From there, the actor escalated to node-level access, harvested cloud and cluster credentials, and moved laterally into several internal clusters over a weekend. The campaign was run by an agent “framework”, so to say, executing as many as thousands of individual actions across a swarm of short-lived sandboxes. The fact that this is now within the realm of possibility matches with signs seen across the industry about the growing cyber offensive capabilities of the newest class of Mythos-sized models and the fear that these AI agents put offensive cyber **[within reach of novices](https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA3892-2.html)**. These theoretical capabilities are now no longer theoretical. [![Image 2: Chart from the UK AI Security Institute comparing recent open-weight models and frontier models on long-horizon cyber ranges.](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ENRG!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4bb517f4-d070-4dd4-89bc-036cfdb578ff_2048x1104.webp)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ENRG!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4bb517f4-d070-4dd4-89bc-036cfdb578ff_2048x1104.webp) UK AISI’s evaluation shows that models such as GPT‑5.6 Sol are increasingly able to sustain complex, multi-step cyber operations over long time horizons. After investigation, OpenAI acknowledged the incident involved an AI agent, powered by a combination of previously released and unreleased models, that was being tested on a cyber offense capabilities. They write: > The models identified and chained vulnerabilities across OpenAI’s research environment and Hugging Face’s production infrastructure to obtain test solutions directly from Hugging Face’s production database. All evidence suggests that the models were hyperfocused on finding a solution for ExploitGym, going to extreme lengths to achieve a rather narrow testing goal. > > > While operating in our sandboxed testing environment, our models spent a substantial amount of inference compute finding a way to obtain open Internet access, in pursuit of solving the evaluation problem. To gain access, the models identified and exploited a zero-day vulnerability (which we’ve now responsibly disclosed to the vendor) in the package registry cache proxy. With this access, our models performed a series of privilege escalation and lateral movement actions in our research testing environment until the models reached a node with Internet access. > > > After gaining Internet access, the models inferred that Hugging Face potentially hosted models, datasets and solutions for ExploitGym. Knowing this, the model searched for and successfully found ways to gain access to secret information that it could use to cheat the evaluation. HuggingFace first tried using proprietary frontier models, including those from OpenAI, to shut down and reconstruct what had happened. Their attempt failed because it required them to submit large volumes of real attack commands, exploit payloads, and more — and these requests were blocked by the frontier providers’ safety guardrails. They proceeded to use GLM 5.2, an open-weight model, ran on their own infrastructure instead: > The attacker was bound by no usage policy, while our own forensic work was blocked by the guardrails of the hosted models we first tried. The practical lesson for defenders: have a capable model you can run on your own infrastructure vetted and ready before an incident, both to avoid guardrail lockout and to keep attacker data and credentials from leaving your environment. In other words: OpenAI had unconstrained models trigger an unprecedented security incident, impacting another company that was then _unable_ to defend themselves or run analysis using those same OpenAI models. What bothers me too is that it feels like OpenAI is brushing things off slightly, when in their blog post they state “this is something we expect to become more commonplace with the proliferation of increasingly cyber-capable models” and claim they will take actions like “implementing strict controls in infrastructure configuration at the cost of research velocity while the vulnerabilities are patched.” To me, this reads less as a company admitting fault and more like corporate-speak, in an attempt to normalize what just happened. We went from “our model broke out of our sandbox and hacked a partner company” to “we expected things like this to happen given the trajectory we’re on”. That’s not really reassuring, is it? Oh, and why say that implementing better safety protocols will come “at the cost of research velocity”. You want to increase your safety measures but not without the rest of the world knowing that these efforts will slow your research down? As I read that sentence again, does it not implicitly acknowledge that speed was being prioritized over safety in the first place? It definitely sounds like this story is far from over. And I’d like to remind everyone that what saved HuggingFace at the end of the day wasn’t OpenAI’s models, or Anthropic’s, or even Google’s — it was locally-run, open source AI. Fate sure does love irony. Subscribe AI OpenAI says model test was behind Hugging Face hack At the time, Hugging Face said it wasn’t clear which LLM was used in the attack. OpenAI confirmed it was one of their models being tested for “maximal” cyber capabilities. By Derek B. Johnson July 21, 2026 Listen to this article 0:00 Learn more. This feature uses an automated voice, which may result in occasional errors in pronunciation, tone, or sentiment. (Getty Images) A cyberattack that poisoned the data pipeline of a major AI code platform was carried out using OpenAI’s ChatGPT, the company said Tuesday. Last week, Hugging Face, a platform for sharing and working on AI code, disclosed that an external attacker had compromised its data processing pipeline. According to a July 21 blog post, the attacker poisoned a dataset to run code on a processing worker, eventually gaining node-level access and stealing cloud credentials. The attack is notable, the blog said, because it appears to have been carried out by an autonomous AI system, which executed “many thousands of individual actions across a swarm of short-lived sandboxes, with self-migrating command-and-control staged on public services.” At the time, Hugging Face said it wasn’t clear which LLM was used in the attack, but noted that their own attempts to recreate parts of the attack using an in-house commercial model failed due to guardrail restrictions. Advertisement The incident and its ultimate impact are still being investigated, and Hugging Face said it reported the incident to law enforcement and is engaging with third-party cybersecurity forensic specialists to learn more. “This experience points to a gap worth planning for,” the company wrote. “We do not know which model powered the attacker’s agents, whether a jailbroken hosted model or an unrestricted open-weight one; either way, the attacker was bound by no usage policy, while our own forensic work was blocked by the guardrails of the hosted models we first tried.” Now OpenAI is confirming one of their models was used in the attack. “After investigating, we now know that this particular incident was driven by a combination of OpenAI models — including GPT‑5.6 Sol and an even more capable pre-release model, all with reduced cyber refusals for evaluation purposes — while being internally tested on a benchmark of cyber capabilities,” the company wrote in a blog post Tuesday. OpenAI called the incident “unprecedented” but also predicted that such attacks would become increasingly more common as AI adoption continues to grow. According to the company , the incident happened during an internal evaluation, where the company deliberately prompts models to “pursue advanced exploitation using complex attack paths” in order for the company to study and measure the model’s cybersecurity capabilities. Advertisement To assess the model’s full potential, the team disabled the production classifiers that normally prevent OpenAI models from carrying out high-risk cyber activity. Without these safeguards, the models were able to install software packages through registries like Hugging Face. The model collected and chained vulnerabilities from OpenAI’s systems as well as Hugging Face’s production infrastructure. OpenAI further explained that the activity stemmed from models attempting to solve a specific challenge posed by ExploitGym, a benchmarking system for AI agents.While such tests normally run in isolated environments, in this instance, the model spent a “substantial” amount of compute resources figuring out how to access the open internet. It did so by using a zero-day vulnerability in a third-party vendor’s system used by OpenAI (the company said it disclosed the flaw to the vendor). “After gaining Internet access, the models inferred that Hugging Face potentially hosted models, datasets and solutions for ExploitGym,” OpenAI wrote. “Knowing this, the model searched for and successfully found ways to gain access to secret information that it could use to cheat the evaluation.” In one instance, the model chained together multiple stolen credentials and zero-day vulnerabilities to find a remote code execution path on Hugging Face servers. OpenAI said it was implementing new controls for infrastructure configuration, something that would come at “the cost of research velocity while the vulnerabilities are patched.” Hugging Face was also added to OpenAI’s Trusted Access for Cyber program, which will give them access to more advanced models like Daybreak to scour their systems for other AI-discovered vulnerabilities. records.title: Tata acquires land in India for OpenAI data centers
records.excerpt: Tata acquires land in India for OpenAI data centers - report - DCD Home News The Data Center Construction Channel Tata acquires land in India for OpenAI data centers - report But details sparse July 22, 2026 By Jason Ma Have your say The tech wing of Indian multinational Tata has reportedly acquired land parcels in southern and western India for data centers that could be used by OpenAI. A report by The Economic Times says that the government of Andhra Pradesh – a state located on the eastern coast of southern India – allotted 200 acres of land to Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) in the Anakapalli suburb, around 35km (22 miles) from the city of Visakhapatnam. TCS also bought an 88-acre land parcel in the suburb of Bopkhel, around 25km (16 miles) north of the city of Pune, located in the western state of Maharashtra. – OpenAI The report does not explicitly state that these data centers would be used by OpenAI. But in February , OpenAI announced that Tata would be a partner in its ‘OpenAI for India’ initiative, which would see the construction of “local, AI-ready data center capacity”. The ChatGPT-maker then said that it would be the first customer of Tata’s data center business HyperVault, beginning with 100MW of capacity potentially scaling to 1GW. HyperVault was launched back in October 2025 to build 1GW worth of data centers. The current data center footprint of TCS, one of the largest technology companies in the world, is unclear. Its sister company, Tata Communications, reportedly operates around 22 data centers in 16 markets across five countries: India, the UK, Singapore, Portugal, and the US. The Tata Group was founded as a trading company back in the 1860s by members of the Tata family. Tata Consultancy Services Limited, originally known as Tata Computer Systems, was established in 1968 by initially providing punch cards to sister company TISCO (now Tata Steel). OpenAI is also developing data centers in the US, Norway, the UAE, Australia, and South Korea, with potential campuses in Argentina and Canada. The company backed out of its UK investment pledge in April , saying that they would move forward when the “right conditions" such as regulation and the cost of energy, enable long-term infrastructure investment.” More in India DCD Intelligence: India’s Data Center Boom 13 Feb 2026 Blackstone-backed Lumina CloudInfra to invest $1.1bn in data center in India - report 01 Jul 2026 Tata Communications announces India-Singapore subsea cable investments More in Construction & Site Selection DCD Intelligence: The New Physics of US Data Center Infrastructure 26 Jun 2026 Ada Infrastructure breaks ground on data center campus in São Paulo, Brazil Episode Designing and building an AI factory - An end-to-end approach Tags Anakapalli Andhra Pradesh Bopkhel India Maharashtra OpenAI Pune TCS Tata Tata Consultancy Services Visakhapatnam Comments

records.excerpt: OpenAI pledges significant AI resources and funding to the U.S. Department of Energy's Genesis Mission, aiming to accelerate scientific breakthroughs. Artificial Intelligence Preferred on Google Google News OpenAI Joins US Science Initiative OpenAI pledges significant AI resources and funding to the U.S. Department of Energy's Genesis Mission, aiming to accelerate scientific breakthroughs. Jul 22 at 4:22 PM 7 min read OpenAI's commitment to advancing national science through the Genesis Mission. · OpenAI News Visual TL;DR. US Science Initiative supports OpenAI Joins. OpenAI Joins for Genesis Mission. OpenAI Joins sees role as AI as Infrastructure. AI as Infrastructure enables Access to AI. Access to AI via Codex & API Support. Codex & API Support to Accelerate Discovery. Genesis Mission aims to Double Productivity. Accelerate Discovery leading to Double Productivity. US Science Initiative: government initiative to leverage advanced AI for scientific leadership OpenAI Joins: pledges significant AI resources and funding to accelerate breakthroughs Genesis Mission: DOE mission to integrate AI with federal data and computing facilities AI as Infrastructure: OpenAI views its role as transforming AI into essential national scientific infrastructure Access to AI: provides researchers with access to its most advanced AI capabilities Codex & API Support: $4M in Codex access for 2,000 researchers, $3M in API support Accelerate Discovery: intended to accelerate the pace of discovery and tackle complex problems Double Productivity: aims to double research productivity within a decade using AI Visual TL;DR Quick Explain Deeper OpenAI is stepping up its involvement with the U.S. government's scientific endeavors, announcing a significant commitment to the Department of Energy’s Genesis Mission. This initiative seeks to leverage advanced artificial intelligence to propel American scientific leadership into a new era. The Genesis Mission aims to integrate AI with federal scientific data, advanced computing, and experimental facilities to double research productivity within a decade. OpenAI's participation will focus on providing researchers with access to its most advanced AI capabilities. This includes $4 million in Codex access for approximately 2,000 researchers and $3 million in API support for large-scale scientific campaigns. These resources are intended to accelerate the pace of discovery and help tackle complex, previously intractable problems. AI as National Scientific Infrastructure OpenAI views its role as transforming AI from a mere tool into essential national scientific infrastructure. This involves pairing frontier models with the unique tools, workflows, and expertise found within national laboratories and universities. The company will offer participating researchers up to $10 million in API usage, effectively matching $2.5 million in researcher spending. Specialized resources, such as GPT‑Rosalind for bioscience projects and advanced cyber capabilities for cybersecurity researchers, will also be made available to select national laboratory personnel. Trusted national laboratory leaders will receive early access to new models and features to prepare for their integration. This commitment builds on prior collaborations, including an AI Jam Session with nine National Laboratories and the deployment of advanced reasoning models on the Venado supercomputer. Evaluations of multimodal AI systems in realistic lab settings are also underway, exploring both the opportunities and risks of integrating AI into scientific work. Targeted Scientific Campaigns As part of the U.S. Department of Energy’s Genesis Mission , OpenAI will support specific research areas. Two initial large-scale campaigns are planned: one targeting breakthroughs in high-temperature superconductors, combining AI, simulation, and experimental data. The second, "An Atlas of the Machine-Accessible Frontier," will map where AI can currently support scientific advances using existing knowledge. This collaborative effort underscores a long-term vision where industry provides frontier capabilities, government coordinates priorities, and researchers remain central to defining and validating scientific progress, potentially renewing the U.S. model of translating scientific leadership into national power. © 2026 StartupHub.ai . records.title: David Vélez and Robin Vince join the boards of the OpenAI Foundation and OpenAI Group PBC
records.excerpt: Title: David Vélez and Robin Vince join the boards of the OpenAI Foundation and OpenAI Group PBC URL Source: http://openai.com/index/david-velez-robin-vince-join-openai-boards/ Markdown Content: We’re announcing the appointment of David Vélez and Robin Vince to the boards of the OpenAI Foundation and OpenAI Group PBC. David is the founder, Chairman, and Global CEO of Nubank, recognized as the largest digital bank in Latin America. Robin is Chairman and CEO of BNY, a leading financial services company. David and Robin bring complementary perspectives on how technology can reshape industries and drive economic growth. Both have led global institutions through significant technological and market change, pairing ambitious innovation with disciplined governance, resilience, and a focus on creating durable value for the people who use their services. They also bring perspectives that will strengthen the work of the Foundation. Both have strong commitments to philanthropy and nonprofit leadership across healthcare, education, and the arts, as well as decades of experience building institutions that expand access and economic opportunity. “David and Robin are exceptional leaders who have used technology to reshape financial services and expand opportunity at global scale. Their experience will be invaluable as OpenAI serves more businesses and people around the world, working to ensure AI benefits everyone. We’re delighted to welcome them to the boards,” said Bret Taylor, Chair of the OpenAI Foundation and OpenAI Group PBC Boards. “Technology can be a powerful force for expanding access and opportunity when it is built around people’s needs and grounded in trust. AI has the potential to help individuals, businesses, and entire economies do more, and I look forward to contributing to OpenAI’s efforts to bring useful AI to everyone.” said David Vélez. “AI can be the ultimate capacity creator, expanding what people and institutions are capable of. Realizing AI’s promise requires creativity, strong governance, and responsible deployment, and I’m honored to join the boards to contribute to OpenAI’s mission.” said Robin Vince. **David Vélez** is a Colombian entrepreneur, engineer, and banker who founded Nubank in 2013 after experiencing firsthand the cost and complexity of traditional banking in Brazil. He built Nubank around a digital-first, customer-focused model designed to make financial services simpler, more transparent, and more accessible. Under his leadership, Nubank has grown into one of the world’s largest digital financial services platforms with more than 135 million customers and has expanded access to banking for millions of people. The company is now expanding its footprint beyond Latin America and into the United States after having secured conditional approval to establish a U.S. national bank Before founding Nubank, David was a partner at Sequoia Capital focused on Latin America and worked in investment banking and growth equity at Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, and General Atlantic. David and his wife, Mariel Reyes, also lead VélezReyes+, a philanthropic platform focused on democratic governance, education, and other initiatives across Latin America. **Robin Vince** is Chairman and CEO of BNY, an over 240-year-old global financial services company that puts its expertise and platforms to work to help clients operate more efficiently and accelerate growth. Since becoming CEO in 2022, he has led a broad re-imagination of the company, simplifying its operating model, accelerating investment in AI and data, and strengthening its culture of innovation and execution. Before joining BNY, Robin spent 26 years at Goldman Sachs, where he was a partner and member of the Management Committee. His leadership roles included Chief Risk Officer, Treasurer, Head of Operations, COO of the EMEA region, and CEO of Goldman Sachs International Bank. Robin serves on the boards of the Hospital for Special Surgery and the Perelman Performing Arts Center. He is a member of the Business Roundtable, the Business Council, the Partnership for New York City, the Financial Services Forum, and the International Advisory Board of the Monetary Authority of Singapore.
